reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: Presents as multiple cafe-au-lait macules with or without axillary/inguinal freckling, closely mimicking neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1)
Crucially lacks the tumour features of NF1: no neurofibromas, no optic pathway gliomas, no Lisch nodules and no plexiform tumours
Caused by heterozygous loss-of-function variants in SPRED1, a negative regulator of RAS-MAPK signalling, so it belongs to the RASopathy family
Inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern; a positive family history of pigmentary features without tumours is a useful clue
Some children have mild learning difficulties, ADHD or macrocephaly, but overall the phenotype is far milder than NF1
Molecular testing distinguishes it from NF1 and spares patients unnecessary tumour surveillance and anxiety
Should be considered in any child meeting pigmentary criteria for NF1 who has no other NF1 features, especially when a parent is similarly affected
reference.pathophysiology: Legius syndrome results from inactivating variants in SPRED1, which encodes a protein that normally dampens the RAS-mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway by facilitating neurofibromin function. Reduced SPRED1 activity leads to mild overactivity of RAS-MAPK signalling in melanocytes, producing cafe-au-lait macules and freckling, yet without the broader tumour-suppressor loss seen when neurofibromin itself is deficient. This explains the shared pigmentary phenotype with NF1 but the absence of the neurofibromas and other tumours that characterise true NF1.
additionalDifferentials: Familial multiple cafe-au-lait macules without a syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Targeted SPRED1 sequencing, usually as part of an NF1/RASopathy gene panel
NF1 gene analysis to exclude neurofibromatosis type 1
Detailed dermatological examination and documentation of pigmentary lesions
Slit-lamp examination to look for Lisch nodules (absent in Legius)
Developmental and neuropsychological assessment where learning concerns exist
Family cascade screening once a variant is identified
redFlags: Appearance of a true neurofibroma or plexiform tumour, which points away from Legius towards NF1
Optic pathway symptoms or an orbital mass suggesting glioma (an NF1 feature)
Rapidly progressive or numerous cafe-au-lait lesions with systemic features suggesting an alternative diagnosis
Findings meeting full NF1 diagnostic criteria despite an initial Legius label
reference.prognosis: Legius syndrome carries a favourable outlook with a normal life expectancy and no established increase in tumour risk, though a minority have mild cognitive or attentional difficulties that benefit from educational support.
pitfalls: Labelling a child with NF1 on pigmentary criteria alone and imposing lifelong tumour surveillance when the true diagnosis is Legius
Assuming a normal SPRED1 result excludes NF1 without dedicated NF1 testing
Overlooking the diagnosis in a mildly affected parent, missing the autosomal dominant pattern
Failing to reassure families about the benign nature once molecular confirmation is obtained
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
management: Confirm the diagnosis by SPRED1 molecular testing and exclude NF1, which spares patients unnecessary tumour surveillance and anxiety
Reassure that, unlike NF1, there is no established increase in tumour risk requiring neuroimaging or Lisch-nodule surveillance
Provide educational support and assessment for the mild learning difficulties or attention-deficit problems that affect a minority
Offer dermatological review of cafe-au-lait macules and freckling where there is cosmetic concern
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal dominant condition with cascade testing of relatives once a variant is identified
